facts.statement: The broad-billed moa, also known as the stout-legged or coastal moa, is an extinct species of moa endemic to New Zealand.
facts.quote: The broad-billed moa, stout-legged moa, or coastal moa (Euryapteryx curtus) is an extinct species of moa that was endemic to New Zealand.

facts.statement: The broad-billed moa is the only species currently recognized within the genus Euryapteryx.
facts.quote: It is the only species in the genus Euryapteryx.

facts.statement: The broad-billed moa was a stout bird characterized by a blunt, downward-curving bill, wide feet, and short, thick legs.
facts.quote: The broad-billed moa was a stout bird with a blunt and decurved bill, wide feet and short, thick legs.

facts.statement: The broad-billed moa showed significant sexual dimorphism, with females generally weighing about twice as much as males.
facts.quote: The species exhibits a notable variation in size due to sexual dimorphism: females generally weighed about twice as much as males.

facts.statement: The broad-billed moa carried its head forward rather than upright to feed comfortably on low-lying vegetation.
facts.quote: Like other moa, Euryapteryx curtus carried its head forward rather than upright, allowing it to comfortably feed on low-laying vegetation.

facts.statement: The broad-billed moa had an elongated, looped windpipe that suggests it produced a deep, resonant call similar to the modern cassowary.
facts.quote: The windpipe of the broad-billed moa was elongated and looped through its body, which suggests that its call was deep and resonant, similar to that of the modern cassowary.

facts.statement: Analysis of gizzard remains and beak shape suggests the broad-billed moa primarily fed on leaves, fruits, and herbaceous plants, unlike the more fibrous diet of the giant moa.
facts.quote: Analysis of broad-billed moa gizzard remains and beak shape suggest that it primarily fed on leaves, fruits, and other herbaceous plants, unlike other moa species such as the giant moa, whose diet was more fibrous.

facts.statement: Eggs traditionally assigned to Euryapteryx gravis averaged 205 mm in length and 143 mm in width, while those assigned to E. curtus averaged 122 mm in length and 94 mm in width.
facts.quote: Of the specimens traditionally given the name Euryapteryx gravis, the eggs have an average length of 205 mm and width of 143 mm, while the group traditionally assigned to the name Euryapteryx curtus had an average length of 122 mm and width of 94 mm.

facts.statement: The broad-billed moa inhabited lowland environments including duneland, forest, shrubland, and grassland.
facts.quote: It inhabited lowland environments like duneland, forest, shrubland, and grassland.

facts.statement: The species was scientifically described by British paleontologist Richard Owen in 1846, initially placing it in the genus Dinornis as D. curtus.
facts.quote: E. curtus fue descrita científicamente por el paleontólogo británico Richard Owen en 1846, quien lo ubicó dentro del género Dinornis con el nombre de D. curtus.

facts.statement: In 1874, German naturalist Haast described the genus Euryapteryx, designating Dinornis gravis as the type species, into which D. curtus was later included.
facts.quote: En 1874 el naturalista alemán Haast describió el género Euryapteryx, designando como especie tipo a Dinornis gravis, donde posteriormente D. curtus fue incluida.

facts.statement: There is an ongoing debate regarding the classification of Euryapteryx gravis, with a 2009 genetic study suggesting it is a junior synonym of E. curtus, while a 2012 morphological study interpreted the differences as subspecies.
facts.quote: A 2009 genetic study showed that the species Euryapteryx gravis is a junior synonym of E. curtus. Following this, a study published in 2010 explained size differences among the remains as being a result of sexual dimorphism, which also occurs in other moa species. A 2012 morphological study interpreted them as subspecies instead.

facts.statement: The genus Euryapteryx lived from the Gelasian to the Holocene, spanning from 2.58 to 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Gelasian to Holocene (2.58 to 0 million years ago)

rejected.quote: As of 2006, half of all complete or mostly complete moa eggs in museum collections are likely broad-billed moa specimens.

rejected.quote: Euryapteryx curtus was one of the most widespread moa species, inhabiting mostly open areas. These moa lived on both the North and the South Islands of New Zealand, and remains have also been recovered from nearby Stewart Island.

rejected.statement: The broad-billed moa presumably went extinct due to overhunting by the Māori, who called them "moa hakahaka," after their arrival in New Zealand in the 14th century.
rejected.quote: The species presumably went extinct for the same reasons as proposed for other moa: overhunting by the Māori (who called them "moa hakahaka") after their arrival on the islands in the 14th century.
